| [THEORY-339](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-339.md) | People's answers to a probability query depend on their own answers to an earlier query whose result it can use: a person's sub-answer predicts their later answer only when asked first, and a bias induced in a first judgment carries into a second only when the two share part of a hypothesis space, so reuse carries the earlier error with it; that reuse saves computation rests on one small response-time study and one secondary-task result | Dasgupta, Schulz, Goodman and Gershman (2018), [LIT-1074](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1074.md), read in [NOTE-875](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-875.md); Gershman and Goodman (2014), [LIT-1056](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1056.md), read in [NOTE-886](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-886.md); Dasgupta and Gershman (2021), [LIT-1077](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1077.md), read in [NOTE-865](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-865.md). In five small online experiments, an earlier answer shapes a later one only when the later query can use it, and errors in the first carry into the second. The authors call this amortized inference, reuse of past computation bought at a cost in bias. The speed benefit is shown once (median log-RT facilitation, n ≈ 50 per order) and otherwise assumed; storage and retrieval are free in the models; the 2021 review adds stale cached values from the planning literature, second-hand. No paper prices when reuse pays or touches stores outside the head. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-349](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-349.md) | For binary outcomes and a fixed representation of individuals, a predictor can pass every test in a bounded class without being close to nature: outcome indistinguishability to tests that see the sampled prediction is equivalent, with stated losses, to multicalibration over a closely related class of sets, a predictor meeting it exists at size polynomial in the tests' size and the tolerance whatever nature's complexity, and learning one is as hard as weak agnostic learning of the class | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum and Yona (2021), [LIT-1068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1068.md), read in [NOTE-885](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-885.md), and Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold and Rothblum (2018), [LIT-1052](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1052.md), read in [NOTE-879](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-879.md). A predictor is outcome indistinguishable relative to a class of distinguishers when none can tell nature's outcomes from outcomes drawn from the predictor, up to ε. With no access or sample access to the predictor this is equivalent to multi-accuracy or multicalibration over closely related classes, and a predictor meeting it exists at size O(s/ε²) (O(s/α⁴γ) for multicalibration), independent of nature. Learning a multicalibrated predictor is equivalent to weak agnostic learning of the class. Adequacy here is relative to the class, the outcome and the features, and is not unique; it is not closeness to the truth, and the papers say nothing about signal detection. | Active |
| [THEORY-354](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-354.md) | An observer's power to refute a predictor depends on its access to the predictor as well as on its budget: against tests that see only the sampled prediction a predictor of size O(s/ε²) always passes, but if fine-grained clique counting is hard, or BPP ≠ PSPACE, some cheap tests that may query the predictor adaptively pass only predictors about as costly as nature's own | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum and Yona (2021), [LIT-1068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1068.md), read in [NOTE-885](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-885.md). Against sample-access distinguishers of size s an outcome-indistinguishable predictor of size O(s/ε²) always exists. Against oracle-access distinguishers, under fine-grained hardness of clique counting or BPP ≠ PSPACE, there are natures and polynomially many cheap distinguishers such that no predictor much cheaper than nature is indistinguishable. Non-adaptive queries add little; the power comes from adaptive queries. The results are conditional and asymptotic, with upper and lower bounds in different parameterisations; they say nothing about human observers or about which access a real auditor has. | Active |
| [THEORY-366](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-366.md) | With a fixed number of data points and a query drawn independently of them, if the variance of the p-th power of the query-to-point distance divided by its mean tends to zero, the farthest point comes within any factor 1 + ε of the nearest with probability tending to one; independent coordinates meet this condition, while data on a low-dimensional subspace, or queries that fall inside well-separated clusters, escape it | Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan and Shaft (1999), [LIT-1099](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1099.md), read in [NOTE-917](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-917.md) from the authors' 1998 technical report. Theorem 1: for n fixed data points and an independent query, var(d^p / E[d^p]) → 0 implies P[DMAX ≤ (1+ε)DMIN] → 1 for every ε > 0. The index m is arbitrary, so dimension enters only through the workload's distance distributions. IID coordinates and several correlated or non-identical workloads satisfy the condition; a diagonal line, two latent degrees of freedom and queries inside clusters do not. The condition is sufficient, not necessary. The result concerns the ratio of distances at fixed n, and does not show that real high-dimensional data loses contrast, or that indexes fail. | Active |
| [THEORY-378](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-378.md) | When items change as independent Poisson processes with known rates and a fixed total refresh rate is shared among them, refreshing every item equally keeps the copy at least as fresh and at most as old, averaged over time, as refreshing in proportion to change rate, for any spread of rates; the freshness-optimal share rises and then falls with change rate and gives nothing to items that change too fast for the budget | Cho and Garcia-Molina (2000), [LIT-1119](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1119.md), read in [NOTE-906](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-906.md). Freshness is the fraction of items equal to their source, age the mean time since an unseen change, both averaged over time and over equally weighted items. With fixed-interval refresh, uniform refresh is never worse than proportional on either measure, by convexity (proof in the authors' technical report). Under a fixed budget the freshness-optimal allocation starves the fastest-changing items; the age-optimal one refreshes them somewhat more. It prices staleness as an objective under a fixed budget: there are no reads, no query savings, no build cost and no cost of a stale use, so it is a staleness term and not a model trading staleness against upkeep. | Active |
| [THEORY-405](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-405.md) v2 | Adding one classifier-free guidance term per concept to a diffusion model's unconditional noise prediction samples images that satisfy several concepts at once without retraining, and on synthetic scenes it composes object positions far better than compositional energy-based models but relations no better; the reading of the summed score as the score of a product of experts holds only for concepts conditionally independent given the image, unit weights, a conservative field and the noise-free distribution | Liu, Li, Du, Torralba & Tenenbaum (2022), [LIT-770](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-770.md), read in [NOTE-597](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-597.md). CLEVR object positions, 1/2/3 components: 86.42/59.20/31.36% against an EBM's 70.54/28.22/7.34%. Relations: 60.40/21.84/2.80% against 78.14/24.16/4.26%. FFHQ attributes are comparable to LACE. Text-model composition (GLIDE, Stable Diffusion) is shown only in figures, with attribute confusion and hybrid objects among its listed failures. The product is derived at the data distribution and applied at every noise level, which [NOTE-597](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-597.md) notes is in general not the score of the noised product. | Active |
| [THEORY-419](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-419.md) v2 | In a structural causal model of autonomous equations, with intervention do(X = x) defined, as Pearl defines it, as a surgery that deletes X's own equation, sets X to x and solves the rest, and with observing X = x violating no equation and amounting to ordinary conditioning, models that agree on every observational distribution can disagree on the effect of an intervention, and in a structural equation y = βx + ε the coefficient β is the rate of change of E[Y \| do(x)], which equals the regression slope of Y on X only when X is uncorrelated with ε | Pearl (2009), [LIT-894](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-894.md), skimmed in [NOTE-696](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-696.md) from four excerpts the author posts: the contents, the second-edition preface, §§5.3.2–5.4.1 and the Epilogue, 46 of some 480 pages. The account is well established and the excerpts state it in full; Proposed because it rests on a skim. The surgery needs autonomous equations and a diagram saying which equation belongs to which variable. The excerpts state the three rules of the do-calculus without derivation, and contain no three-level hierarchy of association, intervention and counterfactual. | Active |
| [THEORY-426](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-426.md) | Evaluating expected free energy recursively over the beliefs an agent would hold after each plausible outcome makes active inference a pruned tree search over belief states, formally analogous to Bellman recursion, which lets the agent plan through short-term costs that one-step agents cannot; that the pruning keeps deep search tractable beyond toy problems is argued, not shown | Friston, Da Costa, Hafner, Hesp & Parr (2020), [LIT-577](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-577.md), read in [NOTE-454](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-454.md) as prose: the equations were not recoverable from the text layer. The recursion is a construction (strong). That it plans through costs rests on single deterministic runs of a T-maze and an 8 × 8 maze. [NOTE-454](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-454.md) declined a THEORY because the results are a construction plus illustrations; this one is filed Proposed under the owner's ruling, stating only the claim the reading supports. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-455](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-455.md) | Every finite stochastic transition matrix on a configuration space equals the entrywise squared modulus of a complex matrix, unitary after dilation, so the Hilbert-space formalism can be written over any indivisible stochastic process as a non-unique representation; within that representation interference is the term by which the process fails to divide at an intermediate time, relative to the chosen configurations, and an ideal correlating environment restores divisibility | Barandes (2023), [LIT-086](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-086.md), read in full in [NOTE-080](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-080.md). Γ_ij = \|Θ_ij\|² = tr(Θ†P_iΘP_j) is an identity (Θ_ij = √Γ_ij works), and a unitary Θ on the original space exists only for doubly stochastic Γ. Interference is the cross-term of Eq. 43 against a would-be Markov factorization, and a perfectly correlating environment that then evolves separately makes the process divisible (Eqs. 45–56). The "emergent" Schrödinger equation is the definition of H, unitarity is a choice the claimed gauge freedom does not preserve, and the decomposition is relative to a configuration basis the paper never fixes. | Active |
| [THEORY-472](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-472.md) v3 | A speaker who chooses words to minimise the information lost about a single intended referent, with words' literal meanings uniform over their extensions, picks each true word with probability inversely proportional to a power of its extension, so the size principle follows from informative communication; in one betting experiment, learners who knew the referent bet on a novel word's meaning in line with the inversion of that speaker (r = .93 on condition means), and in one free-description study speakers' word use followed it only weakly (r = .19) | Frank, Goodman, Lai and Tenenbaum (2009), [LIT-824](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-824.md), read in full in [NOTE-627](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-627.md). The derivation (utility −D_KL from intended to literal meaning gives P(w) ∝ \|w\|^(−α) for a point referent) is a proof under its assumptions. Learners' bets track the parameter-free inversion at r = .93 on condition means (700 web participants); speakers' tag-word use in free descriptions correlates at r = .19, .51 without colour terms and .02 for them. In these displays the informative-speaker learner and a plain size-principle learner coincide by construction, so the fit does not show that learners reason about the speaker. | Active |
| [THEORY-475](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-475.md) | In simulations from the drift-diffusion model itself, with 12 subjects and 20 to 150 trials each, hierarchical Bayesian estimation recovers every DDM parameter with less error than per-subject maximum likelihood, χ²-quantile fitting or non-hierarchical Bayes, most of all at few trials; whether the gain survives misspecification, and how much of the power gain is the hierarchy's, is not shown | Wiecki, Sofer & Frank (2013), [LIT-563](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-563.md), read in [NOTE-466](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-466.md). Experiment 1 gives the lowest trimmed recovery error for HB on every parameter, and HB beat ML on the same data sets in every condition. Experiments 2–3 report more power to detect drift differences and trial-wise covariate effects, but HB was judged by a posterior-interval test and the others by t-tests, and the clean comparison was omitted. All data were generated from DDMs, with sz = st = 0. It is the standard partial-pooling result shown for one model family, not a test of the DDM. | Active |
| [THEORY-489](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-489.md) | Chains of human function learners, each trained on the previous learner's responses, forget their starting function and in 28 of 32 families converge within a few generations to a positive linear function, the bias earlier studies report, whatever function trained the first learner; this is convergence to the learners' favoured function, not shown to be convergence to their prior | Kalish, Griffiths & Lewandowsky (2007), [LIT-820](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-820.md), read in [NOTE-616](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-616.md). 288 participants in 32 nine-generation chains, four starting conditions. 28 families converged to a positive linear function; 3 converged to the negative linear one and 1 had not converged. The bias was taken from earlier studies, not measured on these learners, and stationarity was not established. It supports the claim that human transmission chains settle on what learners favour in this task, not that they reach the Bayesian prior, and it cannot tell sampling learners from MAP learners. | Active |
| [THEORY-515](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-515.md) | Sampling a posterior p(x\|y) when only joint samples (X, Y) can be drawn is solved by a Schrödinger bridge on the joint space, with y held fixed along the path, between the joint distribution and any reference sharing its y-marginal; the bridge averages the per-observation bridges, its first iterative-proportional-fitting step is the conditional score-based model, and the error of later steps at the data end falls as 1/n times the reference's distance from the bridge | Shi, De Bortoli, Deligiannidis & Doucet (2022), [LIT-776](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-776.md), read in [NOTE-589](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-589.md). Propositions 1–3 are proofs, read for structure and not checked line by line. The empirical gains over the conditional score model hold at equal, small step counts on most but not all image metrics, and in Lorenz-63 filtering at 20 steps. That a long noising horizon is not what makes conditional diffusion correct is [NOTE-589](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-589.md)'s interpretation, not something the paper tests. | Active |
| [THEORY-534](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-534.md) | The optimality of maximum likelihood was never one theorem: each historical proof holds under conditions its author left implicit, and of the classical counterexamples the practically important one is a parameter count growing with the sample, while Hodges-type superefficiency is confined to a set of measure zero | Stigler (2007), [LIT-044](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-044.md), read in full in [NOTE-074](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-074.md). Fisher's 1922 proof rests on sufficiency, his 1925 proof on exact normality, and his private 1930 proof on multinomial data and smooth degree-0 estimators. Rigorous treatments (Wald 1943, Cramér 1946) came at the cost of unwieldy conditions. Neyman–Scott, where the MLE of σ² tends to σ²/2, is the failure Stigler weighs as practical; Hodges's superefficiency is possible only on a Lebesgue-null set (Le Cam 1953). It is a history: the theorem statements are reconstructions, and it says nothing about modern overparameterized models beyond one hedged warning. | Active |
| [THEORY-542](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-542.md) | A word learner that infers speakers' referential intentions jointly with the lexicon, and lets words be uttered non-referentially, learns object names from child-directed video more precisely than co-occurrence and translation models, and mutual exclusivity, word-guided object individuation and intention-guided mapping follow from it without principles built in for them | Frank, Goodman & Tenenbaum (2009), [LIT-815](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-815.md), read in [NOTE-611](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-611.md). On about twenty minutes of video from two dyads, annotated by the authors, the intentional model's lexicon scores precision .67 and F .55 against .06–.15 and .10–.22 for five baselines. The behavioural fits are qualitative, the baselines also produce mutual exclusivity, and the Baldwin case supplies the intention rather than inferring it. The reading said no THEORY, because the findings are specific to a small corpus and the record held nothing they correct; this account is filed Proposed for that reason. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-545](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-545.md) | Aerts and Gabora's founding quantum model of concepts is a classical probability model written in a Hilbert space: every context it uses is a projector diagonal in one basis, so the contexts commute and generate a Boolean algebra, its entangled 'pet fish' state gives the same statistics as a classically correlated mixture for every context in the model, and its guppy weights are copied from single-concept ratings rather than predicted for the conjunction | Aerts & Gabora (2005), Parts II and I, [LIT-312](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-312.md) and [LIT-340](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-340.md), read in [NOTE-299](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-299.md) and [NOTE-294](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-294.md). The structural facts are checks of the published model, not of the authors' prose: contexts are sums of basis projectors, counts are chosen to match rounded frequencies, and the authors call the result a "quantization" of a set-theoretical model. Part I's mark of non-classicality (eq. 19) is met by Boolean projection lattices too, and its lattice structure is supposed, not derived. The model as printed is also infeasible in two cells. It does not say that no quantum model of concepts does better. | Active |
| [THEORY-550](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-550.md) | Unsupervised clustering is not made epistemically superior to supervised classification by the absence of labels: it is sensitive to sample bias, highly sensitive to how inputs are represented, and overfits, with the number of clusters acting as a capacity control just as parametric complexity does in supervised learning | Søgaard (2024), [LIT-162](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-162.md), read in [NOTE-108](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-108.md). A rebuttal of two arguments for clustering's superiority, the No-Bias Argument and the Simplicity-Truth Argument, by toy counterexample and by the technical literature on overfitting in unsupervised learning (Hansen & Larsen 1996). The negative claims are firm. The paper's positive step, that supervised classification is "at least as" justified, is under-argued and is not part of this account. | Active |
| [THEORY-562](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-562.md) | In REST2 replica-exchange simulations of intrinsically disordered proteins, high swap acceptance and short round trips show that replicas mix along the temperature ladder, not that conformations are sampled, because the upper rungs collapse the chain; sampling shows only when independent demultiplexed replicas agree in their structural distributions | Koneru, Reid & Robustelli (2025), [LIT-076](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-076.md), read in full in [NOTE-076](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-076.md). A how-to chapter whose one load-bearing methodological point is that high swap acceptance "is not, in isolation, sufficient evidence of robust conformational sampling or convergence" (p. 18). The reason the reading draws out is that REST2's upper rungs are unphysical Hamiltonians on which disordered chains over-collapse, so replicas can swap freely without the chain rearranging. The chapter argues this and shows a passing example; it shows no failed run, and its convergence criteria have no quantitative threshold. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-564](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-564.md) | A bounded generative model can learn its own structure with no machinery beyond inference and learning: spare hidden-state slots with flat likelihoods get filled when an observation fits none of the learned causes, and Bayesian model reduction on the learned prior over states can return unneeded slots, though in a toy concept-learning task it recovers the true number of causes only 45–80% of the time unless the likelihood is given | Smith, Schwartenbeck, Parr and Friston (2020), [LIT-615](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-615.md), read in [NOTE-485](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-485.md). Expansion works in the toy domain over eight runs per condition, and only for novel stimuli. Reduction is the weak half: over 100 runs, the true number of concepts won in 45–80% of runs for four to seven, never for two or three, and in every run when the likelihood was given. Table 1 is the record's only measurement of how often reduction picks the generating structure when the parent model was itself learned. One initialisation; eight concepts, six binary features. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-569](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-569.md) | Measured as the contrast between a set of explanantia's CohOG+ coherence with the explanandum and with its negation, explanatory power satisfies Roche and Sober's Two Likelihood Inequalities for single hypotheses and fails the One, and in one causal chain and one collider it ranks the richer set above the sparser over a range of priors, where no two-place TLI measure can rank a conjunction so | Hartmann & Trpin (2026), [LIT-165](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-165.md), read in [NOTE-168](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-168.md), which recomputed all three numerical claims. One theorem (TLI for singleton explanans sets), one counterexample (OLI fails) and two parameterised existence examples (a distal cause for P(H1) < .7; a negatively interacting cause for P(H1) = P(H2) < .75). The escape from Roche & Sober is representational: a set is scored differently from the conjunction, and the two-place theorems still hold for conjunctions. No characterisation says when the richer set wins, and the paper's claim that the measure "accommodates key scientific judgments" is more than the body shows. | Active |
| [THEORY-587](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-587.md) | A U-turn stopping rule for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo leaves the target invariant once the trajectory is built as a random balanced doubling tree and the next state is drawn only from states that could have regenerated it; with a dual-averaged step size it matched the best hand-tuned identity-mass HMC on two of four test posteriors and beat it about threefold on the other two, and its ergodicity is not shown | Hoffman & Gelman (2011), [LIT-085](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-085.md), read in full in [NOTE-081](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-081.md). The invariance argument (conditions C.1–C.4 and the 2⁻ʲ tree probability) is complete, and so is the O(j)-memory kernel. Ergodicity is not addressed. The efficiency comparison is against HMC with an identity mass matrix on four smooth, near-unimodal targets, and the dual-averaging constants were tuned on one of the four. The account is of the 2011 algorithm; production NUTS has since changed its selection rule, U-turn criterion and adaptation. | Active |
| [THEORY-611](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-611.md) v2 | Classifier-free guidance extrapolates between a conditional and an unconditional score learned by one network; with exact scores this equals classifier guidance by the classifier the generative model defines through Bayes' rule, but learned scores need not be conservative, so the guided field is in general the gradient of no density and the tilted distribution that motivates guidance is not shown to be what is sampled | Ho & Salimans (2022), [LIT-839](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-839.md), read in full in [NOTE-603](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-603.md), with the derivations of Section 3 checked line by line. The non-conservativeness argument is credited to Salimans & Ho (2021). The FID–IS trade-off is shown on class-conditional ImageNet only. [NOTE-603](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-603.md) declined a THEORY because the anthology holds the account of what the guidance weight does to metrics; this one states only the probabilistic point, which the record's [CLAIM-123](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-123.md) uses. | Active |
| [THEORY-614](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-614.md) v2 | If pretraining text is a mixture of hidden Markov models indexed by a latent concept and a model fits that distribution exactly, then a prompt of concatenated examples moves the posterior onto the prompt's concept, and the in-context predictor becomes Bayes-optimal as examples accumulate, whenever each example's evidence for the concept outweighs the cost of the improbable transitions between examples; whether trained networks learn in context this way is not shown | Xie, Raghunathan, Liang & Ma (2021), [LIT-797](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-797.md), read in [NOTE-633](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-633.md). Theorem 1 is proved under Assumptions 1–5 and a distinguishability condition; Theorems 2–3 give roughly 1/k excess risk without it. The proofs were not followed in the reading. [NOTE-633](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-633.md) declined a THEORY because the result is conditional on exact fit to a specific generative model, so it is a consequence of that model, not a fact about language models. It is filed Proposed under the owner's ruling, with the condition in the title. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-617](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-617.md) | In additive Gaussian noise independent of an input of finite power whose law does not depend on the signal-to-noise ratio, the derivative of mutual information with respect to that ratio is half the minimum mean-square error of the optimal noncausal estimator, so mutual information is accumulated estimation error over SNR; in continuous time the causal filtering error equals the noncausal error averaged over SNR, and the identity fails with feedback | Guo, Shamai & Verdú (2004), [LIT-058](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-058.md), read in full in [NOTE-086](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-086.md). Proved five ways for every finite-power input, in scalar, vector, discrete-time and continuous-time forms. It concerns the optimal, conditional-mean estimator; carrying it to a trained diffusion model's learned denoiser needs the mismatched version, which is later work. Theorems 3, 4 and 11 are stated without proof. | Active |
| [THEORY-696](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-696.md) | Under multiplicative noise, members that pool their resources and split them equally every step each grow faster in the long run than they would alone, with no complementarity, relatedness or reciprocity: N independent geometric Brownian motions that share keep their drift μ and cut their volatility to σ/√N, raising each one's time-average growth rate from μ − σ²/2 to μ − σ²/(2N); the gain vanishes as their noise becomes perfectly correlated, and a sufficiently superior member does better alone | Peters & Adamou (2022), [LIT-035](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-035.md), read in [NOTE-059](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-059.md). The mathematics is correct and self-contained, and the paper's own citations show the pooled-variance result was known (McCloskey, Winterhalder, Uitdehaag, Kennedy et al.). Sharing leaves the ensemble rate μ unchanged, so an analysis built on expectations sees no reason to share, and the time average does. It holds with zero cost, perfect pooling, unbreakable pacts and unconstrained growth. It is a sufficient mechanism in that model, not a solution of the cooperation puzzle, and not a showing that cooperation is the default. | Active |
| [THEORY-718](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-718.md) | In a linear-in-parameters model with Gaussian noise and a Gaussian prior, the evidence is exactly the best-fit likelihood times an Occam factor set by the posterior curvature, and when the design grows linearly with n that factor costs (k/2) log n | MacKay (1992), [LIT-623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-623.md), Eqs. 5–6 with Eqs. 16 and 19–20, read in [NOTE-471](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-471.md): for y = Φw + noise with Gaussian noise of precision β and the prior w ~ N(0, α⁻¹I) on k weights, the posterior is exactly Gaussian, so the evidence is exactly P(D\|w_MP) times the Occam factor P(w_MP)(2π)^{k/2} det^{-1/2}A, with A = αI + βΦᵀΦ. If ΦᵀΦ/n converges to a positive-definite matrix and w_MP stays bounded, the log Occam factor is −(k/2) log n + O(1). Exact for this model class only. The general regular case and the singular case are [THEORY-087](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-087.md), which is Proposed. | Active |
| [THEORY-744](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-744.md) v2 | As the kernel width ε goes to 0, Coifman and Lafon's α-normalized diffusion operator (I − P_{ε,α})/ε, for data sampled with density q = e^{−U} from a compact manifold without boundary, converges uniformly on smooth functions, at rate O(ε), to Δf + 2(1 − α)⟨∇U, ∇f⟩ with Δ the non-negative Laplace–Beltrami operator, which is minus the generator of a reversible diffusion with drift −2(1 − α)∇U and invariant density proportional to q^{2(1−α)}; α = 0 gives potential 2U and invariant density q², α = 1/2 gives the Langevin dynamics whose invariant density is the sampling density itself, and α = 1 gives Brownian motion on the manifold, with no trace of the density | Coifman and Lafon (2006), [LIT-1246](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1246.md), read in [NOTE-985](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-985.md), with the PNAS announcement [LIT-981](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-981.md). The paper states the limit as a Schrödinger operator. Written as a drift, it shows what each α keeps of the density: the walk's stationary density is q^{2(1−α)}. On a manifold without boundary the limit is derived in full, the kernel expansion included (re-derived on promotion, 2026-10-20). The paper's own α = 1/2 display has a sign error. Its boundary rate and heat-kernel proof are incomplete and are left to [QUESTION-231](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-231.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-762](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-762.md) | For a reversible diffusion dX = −∇U dt + √2 dW in equilibrium, an eigenfunction ψ of its generator with eigenvalue −λ is closed in conditional mean with no memory: E[ψ(X_{t+s}) \| the whole past] = e^{−λs}ψ(X_t), and so the same given ψ's own past; but ψ(X_t) is a Markov process in its own right only when \|∇ψ\|² is a function of ψ, since otherwise its own path reveals a noise intensity that its present value does not fix | The record's answer to what Nadler et al. ([LIT-1250](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1250.md), read in [NOTE-986](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-986.md)) leave implicit when they call slow eigenfunctions reaction coordinates. Such a coordinate is exactly closed in its mean: its best prediction from the full state and from its own history coincide, with no memory term, and the Mori–Zwanzig memory and noise for it vanish under Mori's projection. It is closed in law only under a further condition. In the paper's examples the condition holds; the mixed Ornstein–Uhlenbeck eigenfunction x₁x₂ shows it can fail. This does not say that diffusion maps estimate the eigenfunctions well from finite data, or that a slow eigenfunction is the best coarse variable. | Active |
| [THEORY-769](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-769.md) v2 | Ownership of a body part is a graded belief that it is the most probable common cause of correlated multisensory input, so that synchronous stimulation of another object moves some of that belief to the object and away from the real part | Apps & Tsakiris (2014), [LIT-1262](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1262.md), read in full in [NOTE-991](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-991.md), with Botvinick & Cohen (1998), [LIT-1277](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1277.md), for the illusion it explains. The rubber hand, enfacement and rubber-voice illusions are read as one inference: unimodal surprise from synchronous stimulation is explained away by shifting the probability that a part is "me". The account fits the findings; its authors grant there is little direct evidence and that it is hard to falsify with standard fMRI. It does not say why such a model is experienced as a self. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-775](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-775.md) | With a Gaussian random-walk prior and an instantaneous unit-variance Gaussian encoder, the KL half of the evidence lower bound is the unordered slowness loss plus a constant; with a linear Gaussian encoder and decoder on whitened input, the bound is maximized on the span of the slowest SFA directions whose lag-one autocorrelation exceeds one half, with the basis inside that span unidentified, and on unwhitened input the maximizer is neither SFA's subspace nor invariant to rescaling the input | Schüler and Wiskott (2025), [LIT-1296](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1296.md), read in full in [NOTE-1015](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1015.md). The ELBO of a dynamical VAE with prior N(z_{t−1}, I) and encoder N(g(x_t), I) is Σ E log p(x_t \| z_t) − ½Σ‖g(x_{t−1}) − g(x_t)‖² − (T − 1)d/2, an exact identity. For linear Gaussian encoder and decoder on whitened input, the maximizer spans the bottom eigenvectors of the difference covariance with eigenvalue μ < 1, each scaled by (μ^{−1/2} − 1)^{1/2} and then rotated arbitrarily. So it recovers SFA's slow span, cut at lag-one autocorrelation ½, not SFA's features. On raw input it trades variance against slowness. It says nothing about nonlinear encoders, about predictive sufficiency, or about Turner and Sahani's model. | Active |
| [THEORY-785](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-785.md) | Listeners interpret an utterance by inverting a model of a speaker who chooses among alternatives by informativeness, so what a fixed form conveys depends on what else the speaker could have said, as the rational speech act account of Frank, Goodman and coauthors proposes | Frank and Goodman (2012), [LIT-821](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-821.md), and Goodman and Frank's review (2016), [LIT-816](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-816.md), present listener inference as the inversion of an informative speaker, the rational speech act account. The record holds as shown, in [THEORY-172](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-172.md), the fits of that model to mean bets in one-shot reference games and Bergen, Goodman and Levy's signalling-game result. This is the mechanism the fits were offered for, filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4 when the narrowing dropped it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-796](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-796.md) | Question-order effects in surveys generally leave the probability of giving the same answer to both questions unchanged, the QQ equality that a projection model of judgment predicts, as Wang, Solloway, Shiffrin and Busemeyer propose | Wang, Solloway, Shiffrin & Busemeyer (2014), [LIT-795](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-795.md), after Wang & Busemeyer (2013), [LIT-834](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-834.md). The general law the PNAS paper proposes, filed apart from what its 66 Pew surveys and 72 studies measured ([THEORY-166](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-166.md)) under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4. The equality is a symmetry of Lüders projectors and a classical model with order events can meet it, so the law does not by itself favour quantum probability. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-805](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-805.md) | Volume-maximizing joint-embedding objectives as a class, VICReg and SimCLR as well as MSN and SwAV, carry a prior toward equal-sized clusters, and that prior costs them semantic transfer when the pretraining data are class-imbalanced, including on naturally long-tailed data | The general reading that [THEORY-306](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-306.md) held before the promotion audit narrowed it to the explicit priors of MSN and SwAV and to one experiment with two to eight classes per batch (batch 033). Assran et al. (2022), [LIT-231](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-231.md), read in [NOTE-850](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-850.md), argue the prior for the whole class, VICReg through an informal reduction to K-means and SimCLR through a cited equivalence, and read it as the cause of the degradation reported on real long-tailed data. Filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4 so the wide form stays a thesis evidence can confirm or reject. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-808](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-808.md) | Transformers trained by next-token prediction on sequence processes whose latent dynamics factor as a tensor product learn to represent the belief state in approximately orthogonal per-factor subspaces of about the factored dimension rather than the joint one, and reach that factored representation first even when noise makes it lossy | The general reading that [THEORY-256](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-256.md) held before the promotion audit narrowed it to the five Mess3 and Bloch Walk factors and the 4-layer GPT-2-style models tested (batch 019). Shai et al. (2026), [LIT-986](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-986.md), read in [NOTE-758](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-758.md), present next-token training (the paper is titled “Transformers learn factored representations”) as yielding factored, orthogonal belief representations; [NOTE-758](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-758.md)'s claims C2 to C4 are each shown on one family of synthetic processes. Filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4 so the wide form stays a thesis evidence can confirm or reject. It does not include the paper's inference that the preference is architectural (C5), which App. D.4 leaves open, or the claim that the factored form persists at convergence under strong noise, which Fig. 12 contradicts. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-811](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-811.md) | With a kernel normalised to unit diagonal, the kernel quantum relative entropy of two distributions is within O(σ²) of their Kullback–Leibler divergence as the bandwidth σ shrinks, for translation-invariant kernels on the torus generally and for kernels on other compact groups | The general reading that [THEORY-313](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-313.md) held before the promotion audit narrowed it to the one kernel family on the torus that the rate is shown for. Bach (2022), [LIT-255](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-255.md), read in [NOTE-837](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-837.md), asserts that other translation-invariant kernels and kernels on compact groups behave alike, and sketches a leverage-score argument without completing it. Filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4 so the wide form stays a thesis evidence can confirm or reject. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-816](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-816.md) | Learners inferring what a novel word means from its use reason about a speaker who chose the word to be informative about the referent, so the size principle in word learning is a consequence of that inference and not a separate rule of generalisation | Frank, Goodman, Lai and Tenenbaum (2009), [LIT-824](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-824.md), read in [NOTE-627](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-627.md), derive the size principle from an informative speaker and present the word learner as inverting that speaker. The record holds as shown, in [THEORY-472](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-472.md), the derivation and one experiment in which mean bets matched the inversion; in those displays an informative-speaker learner and a plain size-principle learner coincide, so whether learners reason about the speaker is open. [THEORY-785](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-785.md) is the same inversion for listeners in reference games. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-818](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-818.md) | In two-scale Lorenz 96 without time-scale separation (ε = 0.5, K = 18, J = 20, F = 10), a discrete-time closure for each resolved variable that fits the one-step discrepancy of a fourth-order Runge–Kutta step as a NARMAX series, with one autoregressive lag, at most two lags of the resolved variable and at most one moving-average term, reproduces the mean, spread, distribution, autocorrelation and neighbour cross-correlation of x₁ (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance 0.005) and, with observations every 0.05, extends the 20-member ensemble forecast lead time at anomaly correlation 0.6 from 2 to 4 time units over a polynomial-plus-AR(1) closure; the model structure was chosen by trial and error, differs between the two observation spacings, and carries no error bound | Chorin and Lu (2015), [LIT-1304](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1304.md), read in [NOTE-1028](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1028.md). A data-driven closure with one or two steps of discrete memory, plus one moving-average innovation, is enough on this test to reproduce the resolved statistics and to double forecast skill against a memoryless-in-x closure. It is the record's first evidence that a short discrete memory suffices in a chaotic system with no scale gap. It is one system, the structure was tuned, and there is no bound, so it does not give the controlled prediction error [QUESTION-222](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-222.md) asks for. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-819](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-819.md) | For an invertible map with an invariant measure, projecting onto the closed span of the whole past of chosen functions of the resolved variables (a Wiener projection) turns the exact discrete Mori–Zwanzig equation into one with no memory term: the next resolved value is a causal linear filter of those past functions plus a residual orthogonal to all of them, so the memory is carried by the coarse variable's own history; a finite NARMAX form follows only by a rational approximation of the filter, uncontrolled in general but exact for a scalar coarse variable of a stable linear Gaussian VAR(1) | Lin and Lu (2021), [LIT-1307](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1307.md), read in [NOTE-1029](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1029.md). Mori–Zwanzig's memory is what a projection onto the present leaves out; a projection onto the whole past absorbs it, leaving the causal Wiener filter on the coarse variable's own history and a residual orthogonal to all of that history. Second-order (linear-span) projections, invertible dynamics and stationarity only. It gives no finite augmentation with a bounded error in general: the NARMAX step is the paper's uncontrolled approximation, exact only in the linear Gaussian class shown here. | Active |
| [THEORY-829](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-829.md) | In Hrbacek's relative analysis, if belief at a context level is credence ultraclose to 1 at that level, the conjunction of any standard number of believed propositions is believed, while for an ultralarge number it can fail: in a fair lottery with an ultralarge number of tickets each 'this ticket loses' is believed and their conjunction has probability 0 | Wenmackers (2011), [LIT-163](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-163.md), Ch. 3 (Stratified Belief, Def. 1; the Stratified Conjunction Principle, Def. 2, eq. 3.5 and §3.6.3.2), read in full in [NOTE-139](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-139.md); re-derived by the promotion audit from finite subadditivity and Hrbacek's Closure principle. A result inside the framework: it says nothing about whether belief has levels, and any explicit level boundary collapses the model back to a fixed threshold. | Active |
| [THEORY-882](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-882.md) | Consciousness in an inferring system requires three things: a unified generative model of its world; entry to that model by a precision-weighted competition that coherent inferences win; and epistemic depth, the recursive sharing of the model back through the hierarchy, carried by a hyper-model that predicts and sets precision at every level; awareness then varies with epistemic depth, not with the richness of contents, and a first-person perspective, a self-model and agency are not required | Laukkonen, Friston & Chandaria (2025), [LIT-1363](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1363.md), read in full in [NOTE-1063](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1063.md) from PsyArXiv v3. A conceptual proposal with no data and no simulation. The three conditions are asserted necessary; their joint sufficiency is argued for AI and then withdrawn for phenomenal experience in a footnote. The formal part (Table 1) is a hierarchy with layer-wise precision hyper-parameters, from which none of the properties the text gives epistemic depth is derived. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-883](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-883.md) | Under active inference, the contents of consciousness are posterior beliefs about the hidden states of world, body or brain, and a posterior is conscious when it has the capacity to inform discrete, counterfactual policy selection, at a timescale slow enough to abstract from sensory flux and with enough precision to tell alternatives apart; on this account no conscious content changes without a change in the posterior, and a stimulus given precision by an attention or saccade policy should reach awareness sooner than a retinally matched one | Whyte, Corcoran, Robinson, Smith, Moran, Parr, Friston, Seth & Hohwy (2026), [LIT-1364](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1364.md), read in full in [NOTE-1062](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1062.md) from arXiv v2. The "hard core" the paper reads off the active inference models of rivalry, access, no-report, interoception and meta-awareness. The first two parts follow from the framework; the criterion of access is "an inference to the best explanation" from what the models needed in order to report. The authors scope it to humans and similar animals and are agnostic elsewhere. Neither prediction has been tested in the paper. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-923](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-923.md) | In a simulated active inference agent, a habit learned by counting the agent's own state transitions and policy choices emerges from goal-directed behaviour, and once acquired it persists, and reinforces itself, after the reward is devalued, while an agent devalued before acquisition switches at once | Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck, O'Doherty & Pezzulo (2016), [LIT-1476](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1476.md), read in full from the CC BY version of record in [NOTE-1138](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1138.md). One simulated T-maze task. The habit is one more policy scored by posterior probability; its prior and transitions grow by count, not by reward. It shows persistence under devaluation, a cached mapping failing when what is appropriate changes; it does not show amortization, and its reaction times are simulation run times. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-937](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-937.md) | When a mixture of experts is trained on the error of a single expert chosen stochastically by the gate, or on the negative log-likelihood of the mixture, an expert that fits a case better than the gate-weighted average gains responsibility for it; on a four-class vowel task, mixtures of 4 or 8 linear experts learned in about half the epochs of backpropagation networks of equal size, at equal accuracy, and divided the task by class pair, leaving all but 2 or 3 experts with mixing proportions effectively zero | Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan and Hinton (1991), read in full in [NOTE-1147](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1147.md) from a scan of the published article. The gradients of Eqs. 1.4 and 1.5 were re-derived when filed. The task is small (two formants, 75 speakers, 25 runs per system) and has two natural subtasks; the idle experts are read by the authors as economy, and their recovery is not tested. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-951](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-951.md) | For independent identically distributed observations, and neglecting how far the log-likelihood-ratio walk overshoots its boundaries, Wald's sequential probability ratio test accepts the null hypothesis with probability (A^h − 1)/(A^h − B^h), where h ≠ 0 solves E e^{hz} = 1, and takes on average [(1 − γ) log B + γ log A]/E z observations; no sequential test with the same error probabilities needs fewer on average under either hypothesis than Wald's lower bounds, which the test attains when the overshoot is zero, and for a normal mean it saves 47–63% of the fixed-sample test's observations at error rates from .01 to .05; the overshoot-free formulas are exact for Brownian motion with drift, which the paper never mentions | Wald (1945), [LIT-1523](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1523.md), read in [NOTE-1165](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1165.md). The SPRT's operating characteristic and mean sample size follow from two identities of the stopped walk, and its optimality from Jensen's inequality, all exact when the walk stops on the boundary. Optimality with overshoot is only conjectured in the paper. The drift-diffusion limit that the record takes from Bogacz et al. ([LIT-569](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-569.md), [THEORY-068](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-068.md)) is not stated by Wald. It is the case in which his approximations become exact. | Active |
| [THEORY-952](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-952.md) | In Wald's sequential probability ratio test, which samples until the likelihood ratio of two simple hypotheses leaves an interval (B, A), the realized error probabilities satisfy α/(1 − β) ≤ 1/A and β/(1 − α) ≤ B whenever the test terminates with probability one, with or without independent observations; so the boundaries A = (1 − β)/α and B = β/(1 − α), set with no distribution theory, give errors α′ ≤ α/(1 − β), β′ ≤ β/(1 − α) and α′ + β′ ≤ α + β, and they would be exact only if the ratio stopped on the boundary | Wald (1945), [LIT-1523](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1523.md), read in [NOTE-1165](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1165.md). The boundaries of a sequential likelihood-ratio test follow from the error rates by a two-line argument that needs only termination, so the test needs no sampling distribution. The approximate boundaries are conservative in sum. Either error alone may rise, but only by a factor 1/(1 − β) or 1/(1 − α) at most. Nothing here says how many observations the test takes or that it is optimal: that is [THEORY-951](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-951.md), and it needs i.i.d. observations. | Active |
| [THEORY-954](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-954.md) | When the information a design yields depends on the unknown parameter, as in nonlinear models or nonlinear functions of linear ones, Bayesian design criteria are normal approximations to expected utility that average a local criterion over the prior, such as the expected log det of the Fisher information, and locally optimal design is the special case of a point-mass prior; a locally optimal design can leave the quantity of interest inestimable, as for the turning point of a quadratic regression on [−1, 1] with best guess ½, where the locally c-optimal design puts half its mass at 0 and half at 1 and identifies only θ₁ + θ₂ | Chaloner and Verdinelli (1995), [LIT-1525](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1525.md), read in [NOTE-1161](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1161.md). Once the information depends on θ, no design is optimal without saying which θ it is optimal for, and the prior is how that is said. The approximations' accuracy is "not much known" in general. The claim that optimal Bayesian designs gain support points as the prior disperses rests on examples, not a theorem, and is not part of this account. | Active |
| [THEORY-956](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-956.md) | In the normal linear model with known error variance and a conjugate normal prior of precision R/σ², the design that maximizes the expected Shannon information of the posterior is the one maximizing det(nM(η) + R), Bayes D-optimality, and the design that minimizes expected quadratic loss with weight matrix A is the one minimizing tr A(nM(η) + R)^-1, Bayes A-optimality; both criteria depend on the design and not on the data, so in this model a sequential design gains nothing over the best fixed one | Chaloner and Verdinelli (1995), [LIT-1525](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1525.md), read in [NOTE-1161](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1161.md). The alphabetical criteria are utilities in disguise, and the utility fixes the criterion. This holds exactly only in the normal linear model with known variance. With unknown variance only Bayes A keeps its simple form, and in nonlinear models the criteria are approximations ([THEORY-954](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-954.md)). E- and G-optimality have no utility behind them. | Active |
| [THEORY-958](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-958.md) | When each view takes pixels directly (a crop of a larger canvas, or the whole image under a region mask), MultiDiffusion's step, the least-squares reconciliation of several denoisers' proposed next states, is their per-pixel average weighted by the weights of the views covering that pixel; this is exact for 0/1 weights, the only ones the paper uses, while for other weights the loss as printed weights by their squares; with a deterministic update affine in the noise prediction it is one step taken with the per-pixel weighted mean of the views' noise predictions; and the guarantee that each view then follows the reference model's diffusion path holds only if the loss is zero at every step, which overlapping proposals that disagree do not reach | Bar-Tal, Yariv, Lipman and Dekel (2023), [LIT-1522](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1522.md), read in [NOTE-1158](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1158.md). The fusion is an average, not a sum: where views overlap each takes a convex share of the pixel's update. The paper's closed form is the minimizer of its loss only for 0/1 weights. Its distributional guarantee is conditional on zero loss and, in the proceedings version, on strictly positive weights, so it covers neither the overlaps as they behave nor masked region generation. Nothing here says what distribution the fused sampler targets. | Active |
| [THEORY-960](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-960.md) | In DeGroot's model, where each member repeatedly replaces its opinion by a fixed weighted average of all members' current opinions, F⁽ⁿ⁾ = PⁿF, the group reaches a consensus from every starting set of opinions exactly when the chain P has a single closed class of communicating members and that class is aperiodic; the consensus is then Σπᵢ Fᵢ with π the unique stationary vector, πP = π, which gives members outside the closed class no weight; two closed classes, or one periodic class, give no consensus | DeGroot (1974), [LIT-1527](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1527.md), read in [NOTE-1157](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1157.md). Repeated averaging with fixed weights is a Markov chain run on opinions, and whether it ends in agreement is a question about the chain's closed classes and their periods. It is not about how much each member trusts itself. The weights are fixed and no evidence enters, so nothing here says the consensus is right, and the periodic failure is a discrete-time one. | Active |
| [THEORY-969](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-969.md) | In hierarchical LDA every document draws all its words from the topics on one root-to-leaf path of a tree drawn from the nested Chinese restaurant process, so the prior is a nested sequence of partitions of the documents, exchangeable in them, and two documents share a topic only by sharing the whole path above it: no document can draw on two sibling subtrees | Blei, Griffiths and Jordan (2010), [LIT-1542](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1542.md), read in [NOTE-1176](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1176.md). hLDA's overlap between documents is nested by construction: at each level of the tree the documents are partitioned, and a document can share topics with two others only if one of the two shares all of its shared topics with it. It is a statement about the model, not about the data, and it says nothing about whether the tree the sampler finds is identified. The multiple-path relaxation is the nested HDP's ([LIT-002](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-002.md)). | Active |
| [THEORY-972](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-972.md) | In the author–topic model the likelihood of a corpus depends on the topics Φ and the authors' topic distributions Θ only through the document–word matrix ΦΘA, A being fixed by the observed authorship, so LDA (each document its own author) and the topic-free author model (each author one topic) are special cases; and the likelihood leaves Φ and Θ unidentified not only up to the permutations of topics the paper names but along a continuum of changes of topic basis whenever every topic gives every word positive probability | Rosen-Zvi, Chemudugunta, Griffiths, Smyth and Steyvers (2010), [LIT-1546](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1546.md), read in [NOTE-1180](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1180.md). The likelihood sees members' topic profiles only through the word distributions they jointly produce, and a small change of topic basis that keeps every distribution a distribution produces exactly the same corpus probabilities. Only the Dirichlet priors then choose among the profiles. It says nothing about the posterior's concentration, and nothing about conditions under which Φ and Θ are identified up to permutation. | Active |
| [THEORY-985](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-985.md) | The beta process BP(c, B0) is the de Finetti mixing measure of the Indian buffet process: given n objects, the next has each existing feature with probability equal to the number holding it over c + n and a Poisson(cγ/(c + n)) number of new ones, so n objects hold Poisson(γ Σ_{i<n} c/(c + i)) distinct features, which is the IBP's αH_n at c = 1 and γ = α, and c alone sets how much objects share | Thibaux and Jordan (2007), [LIT-1537](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1537.md), read in [NOTE-1171](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1171.md). The beta process plays for the IBP the role the Dirichlet process plays for the Chinese restaurant process, and its concentration c separates how much objects share from the mass γ that sets features per object. The conjugacy it rests on is cited, not proved, in the paper. It does not give dependence between features or over time. | Active |
| [THEORY-989](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-989.md) | On the abstracts of the Journal of the ACM, the held-out likelihood of infinite-depth hierarchical LDA is higher than that of flat LDA at every fixed topic count in a range bracketing hLDA's own posterior topic count, about 140, though the authors expect flat LDA to win once the topic count is free | Blei, Griffiths and Jordan (2010), [LIT-1542](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1542.md), §6.3 and Fig. 9, read in [NOTE-1176](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1176.md). One corpus, five-fold cross-validation, hyperparameters integrated out. It is evidence that a single-path hierarchy can earn its constraint in prediction, near its own size. It is not evidence that a hierarchy predicts better than a flat mixed-membership model in general: the paper itself says the flat model should dominate at large topic counts. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-993](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-993.md) | In the mixed membership stochastic blockmodel the probability of an edge from p to q, given the memberships, is (1 − ρ)π_pᵀBπ_q, so the graph's likelihood given the memberships is unchanged by π ↦ Rπ, B ↦ R⁻ᵀBR⁻¹ for any invertible R that keeps the memberships on the simplex and B in [0, 1], a continuum around any solution with B's rates strictly between 0 and 1; and the sparsity parameter ρ enters only through (1 − ρ)B, so it is fixed by nothing but the bound B ≤ 1, and the paper's printed estimator of it is the fraction of absent edges whatever the fit | Airoldi, Blei, Fienberg and Xing (2008), [LIT-1553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1553.md), read in [NOTE-1179](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1179.md). The paper says the blockmodel and the memberships do not compete, because one is global and asymmetric and the other local and symmetric. Given the memberships they do: a change of block basis moves every node's memberships toward the centre and sharpens B, with the same edge probabilities. What can still separate them is the Dirichlet family assumed for memberships, not the graph. The confounding of ρ with B's scale is exact even in the marginal likelihood. | Active |
| [THEORY-999](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-999.md) v2 | In the finite beta–Bernoulli feature model with prevalences Beta(α/K, 1), the expected number of occupied features among N objects is K(1 − (α/K)B(α/K, N + 1)), strictly below the Indian buffet process's αH_N for every finite K and tending to it as K grows, and each object holds Kα/(K + α) features on average rather than α | Griffiths and Ghahramani (2011), [LIT-1556](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1556.md), read in [NOTE-1172](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1172.md), derive the IBP as the K → ∞ limit of πk ~ Beta(α/K, 1), zik ~ Bernoulli(πk), and give K+ ~ Poisson(αH_N) for the limit only. At finite K the count falls short, by 27% at N = 12, α = 3, K = 16. It says nothing about stick-breaking truncations, which approach the IBP much faster. | Active |
| [THEORY-1003](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1003.md) | On NIPS papers (1,557 training and 183 test documents, 100 topics, fixed hyperparameters), the author–topic model gave test documents lower perplexity than LDA while sixteen or fewer of their words had been observed and higher perplexity beyond that; one fictitious author per document improved on the author–topic model throughout and lost to LDA after about 64 words, and an author model without topics did worst | Rosen-Zvi, Chemudugunta, Griffiths, Smyth and Steyvers (2010), [LIT-1546](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1546.md), §6.4 and Fig. 11, read in [NOTE-1180](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1180.md). Pooling by member helps prediction of a document of which little has been seen and costs it once the document's own words are enough. One corpus, one split, one topic count. It is not evidence that member-level structure is real, only that it predicts in a regime of sparse evidence. | Active |
| [THEORY-1006](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1006.md) | In the dependent Indian buffet process each item's feature indicator is a Gaussian process thresholded at the quantile of a stick length that does not change with the covariate, so its prevalence is the same at every covariate value and its persistence is set separately by the covariance; the whole feature matrix at a covariate value is an Indian buffet process only when there is no shared feature-level process, and with one the items are correlated and fewer features are occupied | Williamson, Orbanz and Ghahramani (2010), [LIT-1548](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1548.md), read in [NOTE-1175](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1175.md). Thresholding at a fixed quantile keeps each feature's prevalence at its stick length at every covariate value, which is what a hand-written logistic transition does not do. The paper's statement that Z(t) is an IBP at each t holds for its collapsed model; with a shared feature-level GP it holds item by item only. Persistence for a fixed correlation still falls with prevalence. | Active |
| [THEORY-1008](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1008.md) | Mixed memberships fitted by a fifteen-block MMSB to 871 yeast proteins' curated physical interactions carry information about the proteins' top-level MIPS functions beyond what the functions' base rates give: after mapping blocks to functions on 87 proteins, thresholded memberships predicted the other proteins' annotations with about 87% accuracy, against about 70% for random guessing at the right proportions | Airoldi, Blei, Fienberg and Xing (2008), [LIT-1553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1553.md), §4.3.2 and Figs. 10–12, read in [NOTE-1179](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1179.md). The batch's one check of inferred mixed memberships against labels the model never saw. The reported margin is over a weak baseline, so it shows less than it seems: probably some information, not yet how much. It says nothing about whether the fifteen blocks are the fifteen functions. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1010](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1010.md) | On ten corpora simulated from three-level hierarchical LDA itself (100 documents of 250 words, a vocabulary of 100, sparse topics with η = 0.005, γ = 1), the highest-probability state of the collapsed Gibbs sampler recovered the generating tree exactly in eight; in one of the other two a wrong tree had higher posterior probability than the true one | Blei, Griffiths and Jordan (2010), [LIT-1542](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1542.md), §6.1 and Fig. 6, read in [NOTE-1176](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1176.md). It shows that the sampler can invert hLDA on data hLDA generated, with sparse, well-separated topics. It does not show that the tree is identified in general, or that a tree found in real data was there to be found. One failure is a posterior that prefers the wrong tree, which no better sampler would fix. | Active |
| [THEORY-1012](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1012.md) | Latent features made dependent through a layer of categories, each observation's features being a function of how many of its categories carry each feature, stay finite on finite data when a feature carried by none of an observation's categories is always off; under that condition a category can switch features on and never off, so features depend on one another by sharing a category, or, where an observation has a single category, by excluding one another, and no feature or category suppresses another | Doshi-Velez and Ghahramani (2009), [LIT-1544](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1544.md), read in [NOTE-1184](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1184.md). Z = f(CM) with f(0) = 0 gives correlated nonparametric feature models with O(log log N) expected features for the DP-IBP and IBP-IBP. The correlations are motifs, sets of features switched on together, plus, in the DP-IBP, exclusion between categories; suppression is outside them, and negative correlation is left as future work. The models' predictive advantage over the IBP is mixed in the paper's own table. | Active |
| [THEORY-1015](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1015.md) | Groups of objects drawn from beta processes share features only if the measure they are drawn around is discrete; in the hierarchical beta process that measure is itself a beta process draw, and at each shared feature a group's prevalence is Beta(c_j b, c_j(1 − b)) around the shared prevalence b, so a small c_j lets groups differ and a large one pulls them together | Thibaux and Jordan (2007), [LIT-1537](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1537.md), read in [NOTE-1171](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1171.md). The hierarchical beta process B ~ BP(c0, B0), Aj ~ BP(cj, B) gives several groups one unbounded feature library at group-specific prevalences. It treats each object as in one group, exchangeable within it, and has no dynamics; its one experiment, 58% against 50% on a single text split, is suggestive only. | Active |
| [THEORY-1019](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1019.md) | Under the Markov Indian buffet process the expected number of features on at the first time step is α, as in the Indian buffet process, but it rises over time toward α·E[ln((2 − b)/(1 − b))] with b ~ Beta(γ, δ), which is 9.04 at γ = 10 and δ = 1, so after the first step the rows are not distributed as an Indian buffet process | Van Gael, Teh and Ghahramani (2008), [LIT-1577](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1577.md), read in [NOTE-1199](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1199.md). A chain starting off is on at step t with probability a(1 − (b − a)^t)/(1 − b + a). As M → ∞ the a's form a Poisson process of intensity α/a on (0, 1), so E[number on at t] = α ∫₀¹ E_b[(1 − (b − a)^t)/(1 − b + a)] da. That is α at t = 1 and tends to α·E[ln((2 − b)/(1 − b))]. The number of features ever on is still Poisson(αH_T), as the paper says. This concerns the expected count only, not the full row distribution beyond it. | Active |
| [THEORY-1034](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1034.md) | In the Markov Indian buffet process each feature's probability of staying on is drawn independently of its probability of switching on, so how long a feature persists once on does not depend on how rare it is; the process is defined for the time steps of one sequence, not for several objects over time | Van Gael, Teh and Ghahramani (2008), [LIT-1577](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1577.md), read in [NOTE-1199](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1199.md). Each column is a two-state chain from an off state with a_m = P(0 → 1) ~ Beta(α/M, 1) and b_m = P(1 → 1) ~ Beta(γ, δ), independent, and the stick-breaking construction keeps each b paired with its a as an independent draw. Rarity (small a) and persistence (b) are separate per-feature parameters. It does not say that prevalence is held fixed over time, which it is not ([THEORY-1019](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1019.md)), nor how to share the chains across several objects. | Active |
| [THEORY-1037](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1037.md) | In the infinite hidden Markov model, drawing at each time step a slice variable uniformly below the probability of the transition taken leaves the posterior unchanged and leaves only finitely many state trajectories with positive probability, so a whole trajectory can be resampled exactly by forward filtering and backward sampling, with no truncation of the state space | Van Gael, Saatci, Teh and Ghahramani (2008), [LIT-1622](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1622.md), read in [NOTE-1204](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1204.md). u_t ~ Uniform(0, π_{s_{t−1}s_t}) is an auxiliary variable, so sampling u given s and then s given u leaves p(s \| y) invariant; given u, the forward recursion sums only over transitions with π > u_t, of which there are finitely many per row. It says the sampler is exact, not how fast it mixes ([THEORY-1044](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1044.md)). | Active |
| [THEORY-1041](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1041.md) | In the Indian buffet process the feature probabilities in decreasing order are products of independent Beta(α, 1) draws, so the k-th has mean (α/(α + 1))^k, and keeping only the first K of them gives an expected number of occupied features among N objects that approaches αH_N from below: 8.97 at K = 16, N = 12 and α = 3, against 9.31 in the limit and 6.83 for the finite model with sixteen independent prevalences | Teh, Görür and Ghahramani (2007), [LIT-1627](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1627.md), read in [NOTE-1210](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1210.md). μ_(k) = ∏_{l≤k} ν_l with ν_l ~ Beta(α, 1). Truncated at K, the expected number of occupied features is Σ_{k≤K} Σ_{j=1}^{N} (−1)^{j+1} C(N, j) (α/(α + j))^k, which sums to αH_N as K → ∞. At N = 12, α = 3: 6.80, 8.97, 9.27 and 9.31 at K = 8, 16, 24 and 32. It concerns the prior's expected count, not a posterior, and the paper itself computes no truncation error. | Active |
| [THEORY-1043](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1043.md) | The finite feature model in which each of K features has prevalence Beta(α/K, 1) has, as K grows, a limit on equivalence classes of binary matrices that ignore the order of columns, and the Indian buffet process, in which the i-th object takes each earlier feature with probability m/i and Poisson(α/i) new ones, produces the same distribution, so its objects are exchangeable and the number of features they hold is Poisson(αH_N) | Griffiths and Ghahramani (2005), [LIT-1623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1623.md), read in [NOTE-1208](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1208.md), and their review ([LIT-1556](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1556.md)). P([Z]) → α^{K+}/∏_{h≥1} K_h! · exp{−αH_N} · ∏_k (N − m_k)!(m_k − 1)!/N! on lof-classes, and the buffet gives the same. It is a statement about the limit: at finite K the expected count of occupied features is below αH_N ([THEORY-999](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-999.md)), and an ordered truncation of the same limit is a different approximation ([THEORY-1041](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1041.md)). | Active |
| [THEORY-1044](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1044.md) | For the infinite hidden Markov model the beam sampler reaches the posterior in fewer iterations than the single-site Gibbs sampler, and is less sensitive to initialization and hyperpriors, particularly when hidden states persist and emissions are uninformative, at a cost per iteration close to the Gibbs sampler's | Van Gael, Saatci, Teh and Ghahramani (2008), [LIT-1622](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1622.md), read in [NOTE-1204](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1204.md). Two synthetic designs (an almost cyclic 4-state HMM, length 800, 20 runs; persistent 4-state HMMs with self-transitions to 0.999, length 4000, 60 starts), a well-log series and a text task. The beam sampler is exact by construction ([THEORY-1037](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1037.md)); how much faster it mixes is shown only in iterations and by eye. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1045](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1045.md) | On synthetic data from factorial hidden Markov models with three or five hidden chains of two or three states, an unconstrained hidden Markov model with as many states as the chains have joint settings overfits, its test-set excess over the true model rising to 175 bits per observation at five three-state chains against 4.5 for the factorial model trained exactly, while factorial models trained with completely factorized or structured variational E steps are not significantly worse than exact training | Ghahramani and Jordan (1997), [LIT-1628](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1628.md), read in [NOTE-1203](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1203.md). Four sizes, 15 random parameter sets each, 20 training and 20 test sequences of length 20, four-dimensional, C = 0.0025I, one run per set. In bits per observation over the true model, the K^M-state HMM's test excess is 2.29, 9.81, 11.57 and 175.35; the exact factorial HMM's 1.05, 1.26, 2.51 and 4.49; the structured approximation's 1.04, 0.90, 1.53 and 4.30. It is a result on small synthetic problems the model generated, not on real data or long sequences. | Active |
| [THEORY-1046](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1046.md) | In infinite sparse factor analysis, where a binary mask says whether a source is active at a data point and an independent Gaussian value says how strongly, the evidence of that data point for the source being active, with its value integrated out, is σ̂·exp(μ̂²/(2σ̂²)) for the posterior mean μ̂ and standard deviation σ̂ of the value; when the residual has no component along the source's loading the ratio is σ̂, below one, so the data favour an inactive source over an active one at zero by a factor that the prior on the value sets | Knowles and Ghahramani (2007), [LIT-1626](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1626.md), read in [NOTE-1209](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1209.md). With y = g x + ε, x ~ N(0, 1), ε ~ N(0, σ_ε² I): ∫ p(y \| x) p(x) dx / p(y \| x = 0) = σ̂ exp{μ̂²/(2σ̂²)}, σ̂² = σ_ε²/(σ_ε² + g′g), μ̂ = g′ε/(σ_ε² + g′g). It is the Gaussian case only; the Laplacian case is the paper's (14), checked the same way. It concerns one data point and one source, with the loading known. | Active |
| [THEORY-1097](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1097.md) | A Markov blanket, in any formulation including sparse coupling at nonequilibrium steady state and time-varying blanket states, does not individuate a system: where it falls is fixed by modelling choices made before it is found, so it presupposes the boundary it is used to find, and it cannot represent a boundary the system produces | The wider claim dropped when [THEORY-073](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-073.md) was narrowed to Friston's 2013 formulation and promoted on 2026-10-27 ([ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4: a narrowing's dropped claims go to Proposed entries). Both critiques argue the general form, and the record holds neither of the later formulations it would have to reach. Its promote_when is [THEORY-073](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-073.md)'s own, moved here unchanged. | Proposed |
